Because of their efforts, the wider world is safer and we are grateful for their service. This is the moment we must all say, we are better than this.

This is the choice before us.

I want to be clear: The differences between our governments over these many years are not a matter of some single dispute. The distance between us, the mis­understandings and mistrust, have accumulated steadily, like sediment, over generations. Some of these differences are rooted in history. Others reflect the distinct way that our nations see the world. But at the core, I believe that these differences are rooted in a struggle between two fundamentally differ­ent visions of how the world should be ordered.

For decades then, there has been a stalemate: two peoples with legitimate aspirations, each with a claim to the same land. And so many generations have paid the price. Now, it is time to break that stalemate and finally achieve what justice demands. It's time for Israelis and Palestinians to come to the table and negotiate a lasting peace. It's time to recognize that there are those who would seek to exploit this conflict so that they might advance their own narrow interests.

Tonight I want to begin by congratulating the men and women of the 112th Congress, who have worked hard this past year to meet the challenges we face. Over the last decade, this Congress has found some common ground and worked through its divisions to pass some important legislation. These aren’t abstract ideas. They are real-world decisions made by real people.

The question is can the American people help persuade their members of Congress to do the right thing. Can we come together? It’s not enough for us to simply stand against what is wrong, what is broken. We must stand for what is right, what will work, and what is just. The right kind of health care, the right kind of education, the right kind of economy, and, of course, the right kind of justice for every man and woman. That’s what we are standing for.

America, I believe we can build on the progress we've made, and continue to fight for opportunity in every corner of our country. And it also means a government that is as responsive to the needs of our people as the American people are dedicated to the success of their country. If we do these things, we will not just win the future – we will define it.

It matters to the janitor who can now dream a little bigger and put away a few extra dollars each month. And it matters to all of us, because when more Americans have more money to spend, our economy grows.
